## Proof placement

Claim: "the largest egocentric data collection effort in history" - appears as main subheading on homepage. No comparative evidence, peer review, or third-party verification visible on page itself. Evidence exists external to site: Hugging Face dataset cards confirm 100,000+ hours and 14,228 workers; Mike Kalil blog mentions "dwarfing every prior dataset combined"; but these are not linked from the site.

Claim: "Backed by Abstract, Pear, & HF0" - appears as single line on homepage. No investor descriptions, linked profiles, or investment thesis visible on page. Verified through external sources (StartupHub article, seed funding announcements) but not linked or substantiated on-site.

Claim: "Authentic 3D scans from actual manufacturing facilities, processed with cutting-edge AI algorithms" - appears in feature subsection. No technical documentation, methodology description, or sample outputs provided on homepage. Report.build.ai domain suggests factory-specific outputs exist but page is inaccessible.

Claim: "high-performance 3D rendering optimized for web browsers" - appears in feature subsection. No benchmarks, performance metrics, or browser compatibility matrix visible.

## Claim qualification

When unable to support claims with evidence, the site uses construction pattern: abstraction + imperative. "Build AI on a human foundation" makes assertion without defining what "human foundation" means technically. "Experience AI-Powered Manufacturing" uses second-person imperative to shift focus from proof to action. "Lets talk" CTA avoids any sales pitch or guarantees, instead using conversational framing to defer specifics to contact flow. Three feature subsections stack short claims (3-14 words) without elaboration, relying on visual (point cloud visualization) to do verification work rather than text.

## Conversion path

Reader arrives at buildartificialintelligence.com. First two lines establish company identity ("Build AI") and positioning claim ("on a human foundation"). Third line states the core offer ("largest egocentric data collection effort"). Fourth line adds credibility ("Backed by..."). Fifth element is single CTA: "Lets talk" button (destination and form behavior not testable without click). No secondary CTAs, no navigation to documentation, no sign-up flow visible. Path is: homepage landing -> credibility check -> contact initiation. Reader gets no free sample, no documentation link, no data preview, no case studies before contact trigger.

## Distinctive

The positioning inversion: nearly every robotics/AI company leads with technology, capability, or team. Build AI leads with what it collected (a dataset) and reframes it as a human-centered artifact ("on a human foundation"). This makes the company's unique asset (not the AI model, not the software, not robots) the brand. The second distinctive move: zero engineering copy. No mention of frame rates, resolution, geographic distribution, or annotation methods. Three-word features ("Real Factory Data," "Interactive Exploration," "Advanced Visualization") compress technical complexity into commodity language, suggesting the dataset is so large and novel that marketing it requires restraint, not specification. This inversion of category convention (engineers talk specs, this company talks philosophy) carries heavy weight in a field saturated with feature-list websites.

## Noise

The 3D visualization demo occupies 40% of the page real estate by stated sections but proves nothing material about dataset quality or usefulness. Visual showpiece appears designed to create sense of scale and immersion but functions more as design theatre than proof. "Lets talk" as sole CTA removes friction but also removes specificity: the page does not tell visitor what happens next, what data they can access, what questions will be asked, or what commitment is expected. This matches category noise: minimalist landing pages designed to appear exclusive and exclusive become opaque.
